kind=REMEDIATE
title=Review positions and counts
body=пе́рвый — first. второ́й — second. тре́тий — third. четвёртый — fourth. An ordinal identifies position in an ordered sequence; a cardinal tells how many. These isolated ordinal forms are masculine nominative singular. Learn the position expressed by each form before choosing it.

Ordinals agree with their noun in gender, number and case, like adjectives. восемнадцатую девушку means the eighteenth girl as a feminine accusative noun phrase. The retained example comes from a sentence about photographing her; this displayed fragment alone does not mean She just photographed. The ordinal ending follows the noun phrase, rather than staying in the masculine dictionary form. These recognition checks do not assess producing agreement in a sentence.

For the first ordinal, choose пе́рвый; for the second ordinal, choose второ́й; for the third ordinal, choose тре́тий. четвёртый expresses fourth, so it fails each of those requests. Read the English request: the separately shown Russian cue may name a different position and is not the target to copy.

kind=TEACH
title=Read the full question and the requested information
body=Forms of который do not by themselves identify a clock question. Read the complete supplied question and its noun. Которое яблоко моё? — Which apple is mine? Asks which apple belongs to the speaker. This is the guided ownership/selection example. Которую книгу вы хотите? — Which book do you want? Asks which book the listener wants. The listener is asked to choose a book. Который час? — What time is it? Asks for the current clock time. This requests the current clock time, not which book the listener wants or which apple belongs to the speaker. The independent clock and book cues are different complete questions from the guided apple cue. These checks recognize the supplied meanings; they do not demonstrate independently asking/giving a new time or forming every interrogative. Optional repeated clock gloss practice is separate from the required checks.
dominantAction=Continue

title=A quarter remaining before eight

kind=REMEDIATE
title=Review ages and calendar names
body=A current-time question and the time when an event happens are different requests. The retained event sentences use at-time expressions. A preposition introduces several of them, while the without construction expresses minutes remaining until the upcoming hour. Study the complete source examples before selecting their readings.

Концерт начинается в шесть часов. — 18.00. Она была дома в час. — 13.00. These are the readings assigned by the retained source. The bare six-hour and one-hour expressions do not themselves distinguish evening from morning; the source readings depend on context. Do not infer that every occurrence of six means eighteen.

Я приду в четверть восьмого. — 7.15 – quarter of the eighth hour. Он нам позвонил в пятнадцать минут десятого. — 9.15 – 15 minutes of the tenth hour. A quarter or fifteen minutes has elapsed in the hour leading to the named next hour. The ordinal is genitive; the event-time phrase also has its introductory preposition.

Наш рейс уезжает в половине пятого. — 4.30 – half of the fifth hour. Мы будем свободны в полвторого. — 1.30 – half of the second hour. Both name a half elapsed in the next ordinal hour. Their retained preposition and noun forms differ; recognize each complete construction rather than exchanging endings mechanically.

Передача начинается без четверти три. — 2.45 – 3 without a quarter. Она обычно приходит на работу без пятнадцати девять. — 8.45 – 9 without 15 minutes. Subtract the stated remaining minutes from the upcoming hour. The preposition meaning without governs the remaining quantity in genitive form. These existing choices do not assess independently building a new event-time sentence.

kind=TEACH
title=Month case and date naming
body=Двадцать восьмое августа names the twenty-eighth of August. This standalone date naming uses a neuter ordinal for the day and a genitive month name. A sentence saying when something happens can require a different ordinal case; these checks do not assess that change. The month form in a date differs from its dictionary form. Numeric day-month-year order and the year abbreviation are separate from speaking a complete year in words.

detail=OpenRussian dictionary data is frozen at commit 50e210c4803237779cb562bc1abcea529066031c under CC BY-SA 4.0. The calendar-date examples are frozen at Wikipedia oldid 1357134172. Those license routes are not interchangeable. The admitted calendar-date relationships remain admitted. The three clock phrases are bounded recognition. Quarter-hour lines use a separate Pressbooks notice and do not clear productive clock-time. Productive clock-time is the ReadyRussian Grammar 20 system applied to exact retained expressions for minutes into the hour, minutes remaining after the half hour, and dial reading. The governed span is a text extraction. The clock image, data URI, quarter-hour lines, and linked audio are not admitted. Review is pending.

мне двадцать лет — I am 20 years old. The person whose age is stated is in the dative case: the first word means to me in a literal description. The remaining phrase counts twenty years. The present-time Russian construction has no expressed verb, whereas natural English uses am. This is an age statement, not a statement of ownership.

Compare мне двадцать лет with двадцать лет. The full age statement is I am 20 (years old); the shorter quantity phrase is 20 years and does not by itself identify whose age is meant. The section label age statements names the topic; it is not a translation of either phrase. For a natural-English choice, select I am 20 years old. Ownership of summers and a group of people asking a question would describe different events. These choices recognize this construction; they do not demonstrate independently forming ages for other people or numbers.

28 августа 2017 г. gives day month year: 28 August 2017. The abbreviation г. marks the year after its number. 15 мая 1996 г. means 15 May 1996. To translate the whole date, include the day, month and year; identifying only the month or abbreviation leaves part of the meaning out.

Двадцать восьмое августа names the twenty-eighth of August. This standalone date naming uses a neuter ordinal for the day and a genitive month name. A sentence saying when something happens can require a different ordinal case; these checks do not assess that change. The month form in a date differs from its dictionary form. Numeric day-month-year order and the year abbreviation are separate from speaking a complete year in words.

Двадцать восьмое августа names the twenty-eighth of August. This standalone date naming uses a neuter ordinal for the day and a genitive month name. A sentence saying when something happens can require a different ordinal case; these checks do not assess that change. The month form in a date differs from its dictionary form. Numeric day-month-year order and the year abbreviation are separate from speaking a complete year in words.

Primary grammar https://www.russianforeveryone.com/Rufe/Lessons/Course1/Grammar/GramUnit15/GramUnit15_2.htm, consulted 2026-10-11 UTC: dative for age. Primary ReadyRussian Grammar 24 https://www.readyrussian.org/Handouts/Grammar%2024--Capitalization.html, consulted 2026-10-11 UTC: common weekday/month names and sentence-initial capitals. Retained Pressbooks Diverse Russian traditions grammar chapter sha256 ab2170e37d529a318f395f6e657d8024d0eaed8d7c5c9b34f8831d348b8b76b3: at-what-time examples, catalog/sources/units-16-20/pressbooks/russia-traditions-grammar.html. Retained ReadyRussian grammar20.html and Wikipedia Russia date notation oldid 1357134172 supply the existing clock and date constructions. Primary Cornell https://russian.cornell.edu/grammar/html/le79_86_b_b.htm and ReadyRussian https://www.readyrussian.org/Handouts/Grammar%2020--Telling%20Time.html consulted 2026-10-11 UTC: hour in progress, minutes remaining, dial reading and AM/PM context. Application inference: teach the existing checked names and complete age phrase before practice. Independently authored English 2026-10-11 UTC; final linguistic audit pending.
четверть восьмого — 7:15. The eighth hour is the period leading up to eight, not the period starting at eight. A quarter of that hour has elapsed after seven. The ordinal names the next hour and appears in genitive form.

полвосьмого — 7:30. Half of the eighth hour has passed, so the clock shows half past seven. The compact half-hour expression is written as one word in this retained form. Match the construction to the clock reading, rather than treating the named eighth hour as the elapsed whole hour.

без четверти восемь — 7:45. This construction counts a quarter hour remaining until eight: subtract fifteen minutes from the named upcoming hour. The without construction differs from counting a quarter or a half already elapsed. These choices interpret existing forms; context is still needed to distinguish morning from evening.
shippedText=четверть восьмого — 7:15. The eighth hour is the period leading up to eight, not the period starting at eight. A quarter of that hour has elapsed after seven. The ordinal names the next hour and appears in genitive form.

полвосьмого — 7:30. Half of the eighth hour has passed, so the clock shows half past seven. The compact half-hour expression is written as one word in this retained form. Match the construction to the clock reading, rather than treating the named eighth hour as the elapsed whole hour.

без четверти восемь — 7:45. This construction counts a quarter hour remaining until eight: subtract fifteen minutes from the named upcoming hour. The without construction differs from counting a quarter or a half already elapsed. These choices interpret existing forms; context is still needed to distinguish morning from evening.

полвосьмого — 7:30. Half of the eighth hour has passed, so the clock shows half past seven. The compact half-hour expression is written as one word in this retained form. Match the construction to the clock reading, rather than treating the named eighth hour as the elapsed whole hour.

без четверти восемь — 7:45. This construction counts a quarter hour remaining until eight: subtract fifteen minutes from the named upcoming hour. The without construction differs from counting a quarter or a half already elapsed. These choices interpret existing forms; context is still needed to distinguish morning from evening.

в пятнадцать минут второго — at 1:15. The second hour runs from one up to two, so fifteen minutes into it is quarter past one. Match this expression to the request for minutes into the hour in progress. The next-hour ordinal is genitive. This convention is used up to the half hour.

без двадцати пяти два — at 1:35. Twenty-five minutes remain before two. Subtract the remaining quantity from the upcoming hour. The without construction uses genitive forms for the remaining minutes and differs from counting elapsed minutes.

в двенадцать часов десять минут — at 12:10. This construction states elapsed whole hours and then minutes, instead of naming an ordinal hour in progress. Reading the dial is always available; context or a 24-hour reading can distinguish AM and PM. These selections identify existing construction types and do not demonstrate independently producing a new clock expression.

в двенадцать часов десять минут — at 12:10. This construction states elapsed whole hours and then minutes, instead of naming an ordinal hour in progress. Reading the dial is always available; context or a 24-hour reading can distinguish AM and PM. These selections identify existing construction types and do not demonstrate independently producing a new clock expression.

Который час? — What time is it? This fixed question asks for the current clock time. The noun час normally means hour; its retained example label time reflects this question context rather than a universal translation of the isolated noun. Learn the complete question as a unit.

For the complete clock question, choose What time is it? A question about which book someone wants would request a different kind of information. Repeated recognition of this one question is not independent practice in giving a time, asking when an event occurs, or forming other questions.

Январь — January. Февраль — February. Март — March. Апрель — April. These vocabulary labels name months, not complete dates. Read the shown Russian word and select its matching English month.

Июнь — June. Июль — July. Август — August. Декабрь — December. June and July have similar Russian spellings but differ in the consonant before the final soft sign. December names the final month of the year. These retained forms include the later check targets and their competing alternatives; this selected set is not a complete twelve-month production lesson.

Month names normally use lowercase within a Russian sentence. These retained vocabulary labels begin with capitals; that presentation is not a rule to capitalize every month name. For Июнь select June, and for Декабрь select December. Knowing the standalone name does not demonstrate forming a full date: a month in a date can have a different case form. Learn those constructions separately.

Июнь — June. Июль — July. Август — August. Декабрь — December. June and July have similar Russian spellings but differ in the consonant before the final soft sign. December names the final month of the year. These retained forms include the later check targets and their competing alternatives; this selected set is not a complete twelve-month production lesson.

Month names normally use lowercase within a Russian sentence. These retained vocabulary labels begin with capitals; that presentation is not a rule to capitalize every month name. For Июнь select June, and for Декабрь select December. Knowing the standalone name does not demonstrate forming a full date: a month in a date can have a different case form. Learn those constructions separately.

A current-time question and the time when an event happens are different requests. The retained event sentences use at-time expressions. A preposition introduces several of them, while the without construction expresses minutes remaining until the upcoming hour. Study the complete source examples before selecting their readings.

Концерт начинается в шесть часов. — 18.00. Она была дома в час. — 13.00. These are the readings assigned by the retained source. The bare six-hour and one-hour expressions do not themselves distinguish evening from morning; the source readings depend on context. Do not infer that every occurrence of six means eighteen.

Я приду в четверть восьмого. — 7.15 – quarter of the eighth hour. Он нам позвонил в пятнадцать минут десятого. — 9.15 – 15 minutes of the tenth hour. A quarter or fifteen minutes has elapsed in the hour leading to the named next hour. The ordinal is genitive; the event-time phrase also has its introductory preposition.

Наш рейс уезжает в половине пятого. — 4.30 – half of the fifth hour. Мы будем свободны в полвторого. — 1.30 – half of the second hour. Both name a half elapsed in the next ordinal hour. Their retained preposition and noun forms differ; recognize each complete construction rather than exchanging endings mechanically.

Передача начинается без четверти три. — 2.45 – 3 without a quarter. Она обычно приходит на работу без пятнадцати девять. — 8.45 – 9 without 15 minutes. Subtract the stated remaining minutes from the upcoming hour. The preposition meaning without governs the remaining quantity in genitive form. These existing choices do not assess independently building a new event-time sentence.

понедельник — Monday. вторник — Tuesday. среда — Wednesday. четверг — Thursday. Each word names a day of the week. Match the shown word to its English meaning rather than selecting a neighboring day.

пятница — Friday. суббота — Saturday. воскресенье — Sunday. Together with the previous four names, these make the seven-day set. In the Thursday check, Friday and Saturday are competing day names. In the Sunday check, Monday and Saturday name different days. Learn the Sunday form here before meeting it in an independent check.

Weekday names normally stay lowercase within a Russian sentence; the first word of a sentence still begins with a capital. For the shown четверг, select Thursday. For the shown воскресенье, select Sunday. Recognizing an isolated name is different from saying on a particular weekday: that use needs its own preposition and case construction, which these checks do not assess.

recordType=label
sourceUrl=urn:russian-companion:content-audit-research:2026-10-08
sourceRevision=content-audit-2026-10-08
sourceRecordId=ca-coverage:obj-u17-hours:numbers:hours-rem-body
originalSourceText=Retained Wikibooks Russian/Grammar/Numbers oldid 4371358, catalog/sources/units-6-10/wikibooks/numbers-4371358.txt: ordinal adjective agreement, numeral gender, count noun cases, compound counts and teen exceptions. Primary learning grammar https://russky.info/grammar/numerals?hl=en, consulted 2026-10-11 UTC: ordinal positions and adjective agreement; counting constructions. Application inference: explain existing Unit 17 forms and the requested positions or quantities; distinguish the retained ordinal noun phrase from the full source sentence gloss. Independently authored English 2026-10-11 UTC; final linguistic audit pending.
один час — one hour. два часа — two hours. пять часов — five hours. The noun changes with the count: nominative singular after one, genitive singular after two, and genitive plural after five. English uses hours for both two and five, but Russian uses different forms.

For basic counts in nominative or inanimate accusative constructions, use the one pattern for numbers ending in 1, the two pattern for endings 2, 3 or 4, and the five pattern for endings 0, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9. Numbers ending in 11, 12, 13 or 14 take the five pattern instead. Other case constructions require additional changes to the numeral and noun; this is not a rule for every sentence position.

For a two-hour row, choose два часа. один час names one hour and пять часов names five hours. For a five-hour row, choose пять часов, even when the separately shown cue is the one-hour phrase. Read the requested quantity rather than copying the cue. Recognizing these hour counts does not demonstrate telling the time on a clock.

For basic counts in nominative or inanimate accusative constructions, use the one pattern for numbers ending in 1, the two pattern for endings 2, 3 or 4, and the five pattern for endings 0, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9. Numbers ending in 11, 12, 13 or 14 take the five pattern instead. Other case constructions require additional changes to the numeral and noun; this is not a rule for every sentence position.

For a two-hour row, choose два часа. один час names one hour and пять часов names five hours. For a five-hour row, choose пять часов, even when the separately shown cue is the one-hour phrase. Read the requested quantity rather than copying the cue. Recognizing these hour counts does not demonstrate telling the time on a clock.

originalSourceText=Retained Wikibooks Russian/Grammar/Numbers oldid 4371358, catalog/sources/units-6-10/wikibooks/numbers-4371358.txt: ordinal adjective agreement, numeral gender, count noun cases, compound counts and teen exceptions. Primary learning grammar https://russky.info/grammar/numerals?hl=en, consulted 2026-10-11 UTC: ordinal positions and adjective agreement; counting constructions. одна минута — one minute. две минуты — two minutes. пять минут — five minutes. The noun for minute is feminine, so one and two use feminine forms here. Compare the masculine hour and year phrases. The noun is nominative singular after one, genitive singular after two, and genitive plural after five.

For basic nominative or inanimate accusative counts, an ending of 1 follows the one-minute pattern, endings 2, 3 or 4 follow the two-minute pattern, and endings 0 or 5 through 9 follow the five-minute pattern. Endings 11 through 14 take the five-minute pattern instead of following the final digit alone. Different case constructions require additional numeral and noun changes.

For a one-minute row, choose одна минута. For a two-minute row, choose две минуты. For a five-minute row, choose пять минут. Each other phrase names a different quantity. Read the English request even if the separately shown cue has a different count. These quantity choices do not assess expressing minutes past an hour on a clock.

originalSourceText=Retained Wikibooks Russian/Grammar/Numbers oldid 4371358, catalog/sources/units-6-10/wikibooks/numbers-4371358.txt: ordinal adjective agreement, numeral gender, count noun cases, compound counts and teen exceptions. Primary learning grammar https://russky.info/grammar/numerals?hl=en, consulted 2026-10-11 UTC: ordinal positions and adjective agreement; counting constructions. Application inference: explain existing Unit 17 forms and the requested positions or quantities; distinguish the retained ordinal noun phrase from the full source sentence gloss. Independently authored English 2026-10-11 UTC; final linguistic audit pending.
пе́рвый — first. второ́й — second. тре́тий — third. четвёртый — fourth. An ordinal identifies position in an ordered sequence; a cardinal tells how many. These isolated ordinal forms are masculine nominative singular. Learn the position expressed by each form before choosing it.

Ordinals agree with their noun in gender, number and case, like adjectives. восемнадцатую девушку means the eighteenth girl as a feminine accusative noun phrase. The retained example comes from a sentence about photographing her; this displayed fragment alone does not mean She just photographed. The ordinal ending follows the noun phrase, rather than staying in the masculine dictionary form. These recognition checks do not assess producing agreement in a sentence.

For the first ordinal, choose пе́рвый; for the second ordinal, choose второ́й; for the third ordinal, choose тре́тий. четвёртый expresses fourth, so it fails each of those requests. Read the English request: the separately shown Russian cue may name a different position and is not the target to copy.

recordType=label
sourceUrl=urn:russian-companion:content-audit-research:2026-10-08
sourceRevision=content-audit-2026-10-08
sourceRecordId=ca-coverage:obj-u17-years:numbers:years-rem-body
originalSourceText=Retained Wikibooks Russian/Grammar/Numbers oldid 4371358, catalog/sources/units-6-10/wikibooks/numbers-4371358.txt: ordinal adjective agreement, numeral gender, count noun cases, compound counts and teen exceptions. Primary learning grammar https://russky.info/grammar/numerals?hl=en, consulted 2026-10-11 UTC: ordinal positions and adjective agreement; counting constructions. Application inference: explain existing Unit 17 forms and the requested positions or quantities; distinguish the retained ordinal noun phrase from the full source sentence gloss. Independently authored English 2026-10-11 UTC; final linguistic audit pending.
один год — one year. два года — two years. пять лет — five years. The basic counting forms are nominative singular after one, genitive singular after two, and genitive plural after five. The plural counting form for years uses a different stem: learn пять лет as the complete five-year phrase.

сорок один год — forty-one years. The compound ends in 1, so its noun follows the one pattern. In basic nominative or inanimate accusative counts, endings 2, 3 or 4 follow the two pattern; endings 0 and 5 through 9 follow the five pattern. Endings 11 through 14 are exceptions to the final-digit rule and take the five pattern. Other grammatical cases need additional changes.

For a five-year row, choose пять лет, rather than два года, which names two years. For a one-year row, choose один год; for a two-year row, choose два года. The separately shown cue can have a different count. These checks recognize quantities of years, not ordinal calendar-year dates or a complete age sentence.

The plural counting form for years uses a different stem: learn пять лет as the complete five-year phrase.

Endings 11 through 14 are exceptions to the final-digit rule and take the five pattern. Other grammatical cases need additional changes.

For a five-year row, choose пять лет, rather than два года, which names two years. For a one-year row, choose один год; for a two-year row, choose два года. The separately shown cue can have a different count. These checks recognize quantities of years, not ordinal calendar-year dates or a complete age sentence.

In basic nominative or inanimate accusative counts, endings 2, 3 or 4 follow the two pattern; endings 0 and 5 through 9 follow the five pattern. Endings 11 through 14 are exceptions to the final-digit rule and take the five pattern. Other grammatical cases need additional changes.

Complete raw selected context:
=== Который? ===
The primary meaning is simply 'which one?', though '''который''' is also used to ask about one particular thing in a sequence of similar things.
:Which apple is mine? - '''Которое яблоко моё?'''
:What time is it? - '''Который час?'''
:Which book do you want? - '''Которую книгу вы хотите?'''
Context explanation:
Которое яблоко моё? — Which apple is mine? Asks which apple belongs to the speaker. Choose Asks which apple belongs to the speaker. Read the complete question and its noun, rather than treating every form of который as a clock question. This is the supplied interpretation, not independently forming a new question.
Tuple-v1:tuple-v1:1;35:Которое яблоко моё?40:Asks which apple belongs to the speaker.2;32:Asks for the current clock time.35:Asks which book the listener wants.

Complete raw selected context:
=== Который? ===
The primary meaning is simply 'which one?', though '''который''' is also used to ask about one particular thing in a sequence of similar things.
:Which apple is mine? - '''Которое яблоко моё?'''
:What time is it? - '''Который час?'''
:Which book do you want? - '''Которую книгу вы хотите?'''
Context explanation:
Которую книгу вы хотите? — Which book do you want? Asks which book the listener wants. Choose Asks which book the listener wants. Read the complete question and its noun, rather than treating every form of который as a clock question. This is the supplied interpretation, not independently forming a new question.
Tuple-v1:tuple-v1:1;44:Которую книгу вы хотите?35:Asks which book the listener wants.2;40:Asks which apple belongs to the speaker.32:Asks for the current clock time.

Complete raw selected context:
=== Который? ===
The primary meaning is simply 'which one?', though '''который''' is also used to ask about one particular thing in a sequence of similar things.
:Which apple is mine? - '''Которое яблоко моё?'''
:What time is it? - '''Который час?'''
:Which book do you want? - '''Которую книгу вы хотите?'''
Context explanation:
Который час? — What time is it? Asks for the current clock time. Choose Asks for the current clock time. Read the complete question and its noun, rather than treating every form of который as a clock question. This is the supplied interpretation, not independently forming a new question.
Tuple-v1:tuple-v1:1;22:Который час?32:Asks for the current clock time.2;40:Asks which apple belongs to the speaker.35:Asks which book the listener wants.

Который час? — What time is it? This fixed question asks for the current clock time. The noun час normally means hour; its retained example label time reflects this question context rather than a universal translation of the isolated noun. Learn the complete question as a unit.

Forms of который do not by themselves identify a clock question. Read the complete supplied question and its noun. Которое яблоко моё? — Which apple is mine? Asks which apple belongs to the speaker. This is the guided ownership/selection example. Которую книгу вы хотите? — Which book do you want? Asks which book the listener wants. The listener is asked to choose a book. Который час? — What time is it? Asks for the current clock time. This requests the current clock time, not which book the listener wants or which apple belongs to the speaker. The independent clock and book cues are different complete questions from the guided apple cue. These checks recognize the supplied meanings; they do not demonstrate independently asking/giving a new time or forming every interrogative. Optional repeated clock gloss practice is separate from the required checks.

Mechanical existing emphasis/link-label unfolding only; original words, case endings, spelling and question marks unchanged. No generated Russian, stress insertion, private Penguin prose, media or new source/license declaration. The article has inaccurate introductory language about pronouns/adverbs and conjugation; those claims and unrelated relative-pronoun/mixed example translations are not adopted. Scope explicitly distinguishes these supplied current-clock-time and object-selection questions. Guided apple ownership differs in whole native cue and requested information from the independent current-time and listener-book-choice cues. This is bounded interpretation, not a second native clock-question variant, productive asking/giving time, an algorithm for every interrogative or unrestricted transfer mastery. The separate clock-answer/clock-construction objectives remain unchanged. The three original repeated correct clock glosses remain optional SOURCE_MEANING practice on non-gating GUIDANCE with teaching links and native provenance, not grammar credit. Independently authored English on2026-10-13 within content-audit-2026-10-08; source/rights/linguistic review pending, no qualified acceptance token.
Forms of который do not by themselves identify a clock question. Read the complete supplied question and its noun. Которое яблоко моё? — Which apple is mine? Asks which apple belongs to the speaker. This is the guided ownership/selection example. Которую книгу вы хотите? — Which book do you want? Asks which book the listener wants. The listener is asked to choose a book. Который час? — What time is it? Asks for the current clock time. This requests the current clock time, not which book the listener wants or which apple belongs to the speaker. The independent clock and book cues are different complete questions from the guided apple cue. These checks recognize the supplied meanings; they do not demonstrate independently asking/giving a new time or forming every interrogative. Optional repeated clock gloss practice is separate from the required checks.

sourceRecordId=date-russia:In [[Russia]], dates are usually written in "day month year" (DMY) order. This o
originalSourceText=In [[Russia]], dates are usually written in "day month year" (DMY) order. This order is used in both the all-numeric date (for example "{{lang|ru|28.08.17}}") and the expanded form (for example "{{lang|ru|28 августа 2017 г.}}"); the trailing "г" is short for "года" (''goda'', "of the year"). Coincidentally, in Polish the word for year is "rok", so a similar date format is used by the Poles e.g. 1987r). Single-digit numbers for day or month may have a preceding zero (for example "{{lang|ru|28.08.2017}}") is more usual.

When saying the date, it is usually pronounced using the ordinal number of the day first (in neutral [[grammatical gender]]), then the month in [[genitive case]] (for example "{{lang|ru|Двадцать восьмое августа}}").

recordType=meaning
sourceUrl=https://www.readyrussian.org/Handouts/Grammar%2020--Telling%20Time.html
sourceRevision=b6702e45884f1ab6ec0334c884393f23f1d61a7ed1fa3d764508ef1de9cd87ff
sourceRecordId=grammar20:We can read off the numbers shown on the dial. When we do so we are stating the 
originalSourceText=We can read off the numbers shown on the dial. When we do so we are stating the number of whole hours and minutes which have passed since noon or midnight. This option is always available.
In Russian we can state the number of minutes into the hour which is in progress. This makes sense up to the half hour.
We can say how many minutes remain until the little hand passes the next number on the dial. This is used after the half hour.
We can speak of quarters and halves of an hour rather than of minutes.
If the precise time is not important, then in Russian we can say things like “at the beginning of the hour” to indicate a time close to the start of the our or “at the end of the hour” for a time near its end.

The concept of the hour in progress will be unfamiliar to most English speakers. It is important to understand that “the first hour” does not mean one o'clock. It means the sixty-minute period which starts at 12 o'clock and ends at one o'clock. In the examples below the hour in progress is represented by a shaded pie slice.

The first hour began at 12 o'clock. To say that something happens at the time shown at left:
в двенадцать часов десять минут—at twelve hours ten minutes
в десять минут первого—at ten minutes of the first
в начале первого часа—at the beginning of the first hour

As the little hand passes the 1 the first hour ends and the second begins. To specify this time use any of these expressions:
в час пятнадцать минут—at [one] hour fifteen minutes
в пятнадцать минут второго—at the fifteenth minute of the second [hour]

в час двадцать пять минут—at [one] hour twenty five minutes
в двадцать пять минут второго—at twenty five minutes of the second [hour]

Once the hour is half-way done we may choose to say how soon the little hand will pass the next number. To specify the time shown at left:
в час тридцать пять минут—at [one] hour thirty five minutes
без двадцати пяти два—lacking twenty five minutes to the two
shippedText=at the fifteenth minute of the second [hour]

sourceRevision=b6702e45884f1ab6ec0334c884393f23f1d61a7ed1fa3d764508ef1de9cd87ff
sourceRecordId=grammar20:We can read off the numbers shown on the dial. When we do so we are stating the 
originalSourceText=We can read off the numbers shown on the dial. When we do so we are stating the number of whole hours and minutes which have passed since noon or midnight. This option is always available.
In Russian we can state the number of minutes into the hour which is in progress. This makes sense up to the half hour.
We can say how many minutes remain until the little hand passes the next number on the dial. This is used after the half hour.
We can speak of quarters and halves of an hour rather than of minutes.
If the precise time is not important, then in Russian we can say things like “at the beginning of the hour” to indicate a time close to the start of the our or “at the end of the hour” for a time near its end.

The concept of the hour in progress will be unfamiliar to most English speakers. It is important to understand that “the first hour” does not mean one o'clock. It means the sixty-minute period which starts at 12 o'clock and ends at one o'clock. In the examples below the hour in progress is represented by a shaded pie slice.

The first hour began at 12 o'clock. To say that something happens at the time shown at left:
в двенадцать часов десять минут—at twelve hours ten minutes
в десять минут первого—at ten minutes of the first
в начале первого часа—at the beginning of the first hour

As the little hand passes the 1 the first hour ends and the second begins. To specify this time use any of these expressions:
в час пятнадцать минут—at [one] hour fifteen minutes
в пятнадцать минут второго—at the fifteenth minute of the second [hour]

в час двадцать пять минут—at [one] hour twenty five minutes
в двадцать пять минут второго—at twenty five minutes of the second [hour]

Once the hour is half-way done we may choose to say how soon the little hand will pass the next number. To specify the time shown at left:
в час тридцать пять минут—at [one] hour thirty five minutes
без двадцати пяти два—lacking twenty five minutes to the two
shippedText=lacking twenty five minutes to the two

recordType=meaning
sourceUrl=https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Russian/Numbers?oldid=4371358
sourceRevision=4371358
sourceRecordId=numbers:==Ordinal numbers==

Ordinal numerals in Russian are relatively easy to deal wit
originalSourceText===Ordinal numbers==

Ordinal numerals in Russian are relatively easy to deal with.  They all decline like adjectives.  For example: Только что фотографировала восемнадцатую девушку (She just photographed the eighteenth girl).

# п'''е'''рвый, п'''е'''рвая, п'''е'''рвое
# втор'''о'''й, втор'''а'''я, втор'''о'''е
# тр'''е'''тий, тр'''е'''тья, тр'''е'''тье
# четв'''ё'''ртый

recordType=meaning
sourceUrl=https://wisc.pb.unizin.org/diverserussian/chapter/russia-traditions-grammar/
sourceRevision=ab2170e37d529a318f395f6e657d8024d0eaed8d7c5c9b34f8831d348b8b76b3
sourceRecordId=pressbooks-traditions-grammar:Грамматика: At what time on the quarter hour</strong></p>
</header>
<div class="
originalSourceText=Грамматика: At what time on the quarter hour</strong></p>
</header>
<div class="textbox__content">
<table class="grid" style="border-collapse: collapse;width: 100%">
<thead>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>Time</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%"><strong>Explanation and examples</strong></td>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the hour (0.00)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>в</strong> + accusative, but note that the number then often requires genitive case after it. In informal speech, sometimes people leave out час / часа / часов. Remember: один час; два / три / четыре часа; пять часов.
<p>Концерт начинается <strong>в шесть часов</strong>. (18.00)<br>
Она была дома <strong>в час</strong>. (13.00)</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the quarter hour (0.15)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>в</strong> + accusative with either <strong>четверть</strong> (quarter) or <strong>пятнадцать минут</strong>. Then you use the ordinal number of the next hour in the genitive case. In essence you are saying quarter of the next hour. Note that while you can say 6:15 as “шесть пятнадцать”, in the exercises on this page we would like to focus on this other way of expressing the time.
<p>Я приду <strong>в четверть восьмого</strong>. (7.15 – quarter of the eighth hour)<br>
Он нам позвонил <strong>в пятнадцать минут десятого</strong>. (9.15 – 15 minutes of the tenth hour)</p>
<p>If you need to review the ordinal numbers up to twelve, you can find them here:</p>
<div id="h5p-256">
<div class="h5p-iframe-wrapper"><iframe id="h5p-iframe-256" class="h5p-iframe" data-content-id="256" style="height:1px" src="about:blank" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="Ordinal numbers"></iframe></div>
</div>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the half hour (0.30)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>в</strong> + prepositional with <strong>половина</strong> and the genitive case of the ordinal number of the next hour, or colloquially, <strong>пол_____</strong> (genitive case of the ordinal number of the next hour). Note that the spelling of 10:30 adds a hyphen: пол-одиннадцатого.
<p>Наш рейс уезжает <strong>в половине пятого</strong>. (4.30 – half of the fifth hour)<br>
Мы будем свободны <strong>в полвторого</strong>. (1.30 – half of the second hour)</p>
<p>If you need to review the ordinal numbers up to twelve, you can find them here:</p>
<div id="h5p-256">
<div class="h5p-iframe-wrapper"><iframe id="h5p-iframe-256" class="h5p-iframe" data-content-id="256" style="height:1px" src="about:blank" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="Ordinal numbers"></iframe></div>
</div>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the three quarters hour (0.45)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>без</strong> + genitive with <strong>четверть</strong> or <strong>пятнадцать минут</strong>. Then you use the cardinal number of the next hour in the nominative case. In essence you are saying X hours without X minutes.
<p>Передача начинается <strong>без четверти три</strong>. (2.45 – 3 without a quarter)<br>
Она обычно приходит на работу <strong>без пятнадцати девять</strong>. (8.45 – 9 without 15 minutes)</p>

<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>в</strong> + accusative, but note that the number then often requires genitive case after it. In informal speech, sometimes people leave out час / часа / часов. Remember: один час; два / три / четыре часа; пять часов.
<p>Концерт начинается <strong>в шесть часов</strong>. (18.00)<br>
Она была дома <strong>в час</strong>. (13.00)</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the quarter hour (0.15)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>в</strong> + accusative with either <strong>четверть</strong> (quarter) or <strong>пятнадцать минут</strong>. Then you use the ordinal number of the next hour in the genitive case. In essence you are saying quarter of the next hour. Note that while you can say 6:15 as “шесть пятнадцать”, in the exercises on this page we would like to focus on this other way of expressing the time.
<p>Я приду <strong>в четверть восьмого</strong>. (7.15 – quarter of the eighth hour)<br>
Он нам позвонил <strong>в пятнадцать минут десятого</strong>. (9.15 – 15 minutes of the tenth hour)</p>
<p>If you need to review the ordinal numbers up to twelve, you can find them here:</p>

<div class="h5p-iframe-wrapper"><iframe id="h5p-iframe-256" class="h5p-iframe" data-content-id="256" style="height:1px" src="about:blank" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="Ordinal numbers"></iframe></div>
</div>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the half hour (0.30)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>в</strong> + prepositional with <strong>половина</strong> and the genitive case of the ordinal number of the next hour, or colloquially, <strong>пол_____</strong> (genitive case of the ordinal number of the next hour). Note that the spelling of 10:30 adds a hyphen: пол-одиннадцатого.
<p>Наш рейс уезжает <strong>в половине пятого</strong>. (4.30 – half of the fifth hour)<br>
Мы будем свободны <strong>в полвторого</strong>. (1.30 – half of the second hour)</p>
<p>If you need to review the ordinal numbers up to twelve, you can find them here:</p>

</header>
<div class="textbox__content">

<thead>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>Time</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%"><strong>Explanation and examples</strong></td>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the hour (0.00)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>в</strong> + accusative, but note that the number then often requires genitive case after it. In informal speech, sometimes people leave out час / часа / часов. Remember: один час; два / три / четыре часа; пять часов.
<p>Концерт начинается <strong>в шесть часов</strong>. (18.00)<br>
Она была дома <strong>в час</strong>. (13.00)</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the quarter hour (0.15)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>в</strong> + accusative with either <strong>четверть</strong> (quarter) or <strong>пятнадцать минут</strong>. Then you use the ordinal number of the next hour in the genitive case. In essence you are saying quarter of the next hour. Note that while you can say 6:15 as “шесть пятнадцать”, in the exercises on this page we would like to focus on this other way of expressing the time.
<p>Я приду <strong>в четверть восьмого</strong>. (7.15 – quarter of the eighth hour)<br>
Он нам позвонил <strong>в пятнадцать минут десятого</strong>. (9.15 – 15 minutes of the tenth hour)</p>

</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the half hour (0.30)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>в</strong> + prepositional with <strong>половина</strong> and the genitive case of the ordinal number of the next hour, or colloquially, <strong>пол_____</strong> (genitive case of the ordinal number of the next hour). Note that the spelling of 10:30 adds a hyphen: пол-одиннадцатого.
<p>Наш рейс уезжает <strong>в половине пятого</strong>. (4.30 – half of the fifth hour)<br>
Мы будем свободны <strong>в полвторого</strong>. (1.30 – half of the second hour)</p>
<p>If you need to review the ordinal numbers up to twelve, you can find them here:</p>

<div class="h5p-iframe-wrapper"><iframe id="h5p-iframe-256" class="h5p-iframe" data-content-id="256" style="height:1px" src="about:blank" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="Ordinal numbers"></iframe></div>
</div>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the three quarters hour (0.45)</strong></td>

<p>Передача начинается <strong>без четверти три</strong>. (2.45 – 3 without a quarter)<br>

originalSourceText=Russians don't capitalize days of the week.

{|
|-
| день || noun || day || dyehn
|-
| colspan="4" | A cognate (same word in Russian and English).
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| сегодня || noun || today || sevódnya
|-
| colspan="4" | The г here is pronounced as a в. It sounds like "с его дня", which would mean "from his day", if день were an animate noun. But it's not.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| понедельник || noun || Monday || ponyedyél'nik
|-
| colspan="4" | On Mondays we ride our ''ponies'' to ''Nick's deli''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| вторник || noun || Tuesday || vtórnik
|-
| colspan="4" | On Tuesdays we go to the ''store'' with ''Nick''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| среда || noun || Wednesday || sryéda
|-
| colspan="4" | Wednesdays are a good day for ''shredding''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| четверг || noun || Thursday || chetvérg
|-
| colspan="4" | On Thursdays ''Chet'' goes to ''work''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| пятница || noun || Friday || pyátnitsa
|-
| colspan="4" | "On Fridays we eat ''pizza'' on a ''yacht'', ''neatly''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| суббота || noun || Saturday || soobbóta
|-
| colspan="4" | "On Saturdays ''Sue'' goes ''boating''. Also Saturday is the ''Sabbath''. Don't confuse суббота with собакa, that is a dog.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| воскресенье || noun || Sunday

sourceRevision=3594124
sourceRecordId=days:Russians don't capitalize days of the week.

{|
|-
| день || noun || day || dyeh
originalSourceText=Russians don't capitalize days of the week.

{|
|-
| день || noun || day || dyehn
|-
| colspan="4" | A cognate (same word in Russian and English).
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| сегодня || noun || today || sevódnya
|-
| colspan="4" | The г here is pronounced as a в. It sounds like "с его дня", which would mean "from his day", if день were an animate noun. But it's not.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| понедельник || noun || Monday || ponyedyél'nik
|-
| colspan="4" | On Mondays we ride our ''ponies'' to ''Nick's deli''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| вторник || noun || Tuesday || vtórnik
|-
| colspan="4" | On Tuesdays we go to the ''store'' with ''Nick''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| среда || noun || Wednesday || sryéda
|-
| colspan="4" | Wednesdays are a good day for ''shredding''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| четверг || noun || Thursday || chetvérg
|-
| colspan="4" | On Thursdays ''Chet'' goes to ''work''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| пятница || noun || Friday || pyátnitsa
|-
| colspan="4" | "On Fridays we eat ''pizza'' on a ''yacht'', ''neatly''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| суббота || noun || Saturday || soobbóta
|-
| colspan="4" | "On Saturdays ''Sue'' goes ''boating''. Also Saturday is the ''Sabbath''. Don't confuse суббота with собакa, that is a dog.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| воскресенье || noun || Sunday

recordType=instruction

sourceRevision=1357134172
sourceRecordId=date-russia:In [[Russia]], dates are usually written in "day month year" (DMY) order. This o
originalSourceText=In [[Russia]], dates are usually written in "day month year" (DMY) order. This order is used in both the all-numeric date (for example "{{lang|ru|28.08.17}}") and the expanded form (for example "{{lang|ru|28 августа 2017 г.}}"); the trailing "г" is short for "года" (''goda'', "of the year"). Coincidentally, in Polish the word for year is "rok", so a similar date format is used by the Poles e.g. 1987r). Single-digit numbers for day or month may have a preceding zero (for example "{{lang|ru|28.08.2017}}") is more usual.

When saying the date, it is usually pronounced using the ordinal number of the day first (in neutral [[grammatical gender]]), then the month in [[genitive case]] (for example "{{lang|ru|Двадцать восьмое августа}}").
shippedText=In Russia, dates are usually written in "day month year" (DMY) order. This order is used in both the all-numeric date (for example "28.08.17") and the expanded form (for example "28 августа 2017 г."); the trailing "г" is short for "года" (goda, "of the year"). Coincidentally, in Polish the word for year is "rok", so a similar date format is used by the Poles e.g. 1987r). Single-digit numbers for day or month may have a preceding zero (for example "28.08.2017") is more usual.

When saying the date, it is usually pronounced using the ordinal number of the day first (in neutral grammatical gender), then the month in genitive case (for example "Двадцать восьмое августа").

sourceRecordId=date-russia:In [[Russia]], dates are usually written in "day month year" (DMY) order. This o
originalSourceText=In [[Russia]], dates are usually written in "day month year" (DMY) order. This order is used in both the all-numeric date (for example "{{lang|ru|28.08.17}}") and the expanded form (for example "{{lang|ru|28 августа 2017 г.}}"); the trailing "г" is short for "года" (''goda'', "of the year"). Coincidentally, in Polish the word for year is "rok", so a similar date format is used by the Poles e.g. 1987r). Single-digit numbers for day or month may have a preceding zero (for example "{{lang|ru|28.08.2017}}") is more usual.

When saying the date, it is usually pronounced using the ordinal number of the day first (in neutral [[grammatical gender]]), then the month in [[genitive case]] (for example "{{lang|ru|Двадцать восьмое августа}}").

recordType=instruction
sourceUrl=https://www.readyrussian.org/Handouts/Grammar%2020--Telling%20Time.html
sourceRevision=b6702e45884f1ab6ec0334c884393f23f1d61a7ed1fa3d764508ef1de9cd87ff
sourceRecordId=grammar20:We can read off the numbers shown on the dial. When we do so we are stating the 
originalSourceText=We can read off the numbers shown on the dial. When we do so we are stating the number of whole hours and minutes which have passed since noon or midnight. This option is always available.
In Russian we can state the number of minutes into the hour which is in progress. This makes sense up to the half hour.
We can say how many minutes remain until the little hand passes the next number on the dial. This is used after the half hour.
We can speak of quarters and halves of an hour rather than of minutes.
If the precise time is not important, then in Russian we can say things like “at the beginning of the hour” to indicate a time close to the start of the our or “at the end of the hour” for a time near its end.

The concept of the hour in progress will be unfamiliar to most English speakers. It is important to understand that “the first hour” does not mean one o'clock. It means the sixty-minute period which starts at 12 o'clock and ends at one o'clock. In the examples below the hour in progress is represented by a shaded pie slice.

The first hour began at 12 o'clock. To say that something happens at the time shown at left:
в двенадцать часов десять минут—at twelve hours ten minutes
в десять минут первого—at ten minutes of the first
в начале первого часа—at the beginning of the first hour

As the little hand passes the 1 the first hour ends and the second begins. To specify this time use any of these expressions:
в час пятнадцать минут—at [one] hour fifteen minutes
в пятнадцать минут второго—at the fifteenth minute of the second [hour]

в час двадцать пять минут—at [one] hour twenty five minutes
в двадцать пять минут второго—at twenty five minutes of the second [hour]

Once the hour is half-way done we may choose to say how soon the little hand will pass the next number. To specify the time shown at left:
в час тридцать пять минут—at [one] hour thirty five minutes
без двадцати пяти два—lacking twenty five minutes to the two
shippedText=In Russian we can state the number of minutes into the hour which is in progress.

We can say how many minutes remain until the little hand passes the next number on the dial. This is used after the half hour.
We can speak of quarters and halves of an hour rather than of minutes.
If the precise time is not important, then in Russian we can say things like “at the beginning of the hour” to indicate a time close to the start of the our or “at the end of the hour” for a time near its end.

The concept of the hour in progress will be unfamiliar to most English speakers. It is important to understand that “the first hour” does not mean one o'clock. It means the sixty-minute period which starts at 12 o'clock and ends at one o'clock. In the examples below the hour in progress is represented by a shaded pie slice.

The first hour began at 12 o'clock. To say that something happens at the time shown at left:
в двенадцать часов десять минут—at twelve hours ten minutes
в десять минут первого—at ten minutes of the first
в начале первого часа—at the beginning of the first hour

As the little hand passes the 1 the first hour ends and the second begins. To specify this time use any of these expressions:
в час пятнадцать минут—at [one] hour fifteen minutes
в пятнадцать минут второго—at the fifteenth minute of the second [hour]

в час двадцать пять минут—at [one] hour twenty five minutes
в двадцать пять минут второго—at twenty five minutes of the second [hour]

Once the hour is half-way done we may choose to say how soon the little hand will pass the next number. To specify the time shown at left:
в час тридцать пять минут—at [one] hour thirty five minutes
без двадцати пяти два—lacking twenty five minutes to the two
shippedText=at [one] hour fifteen minutes

recordType=instruction
sourceUrl=https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Russian/Numbers?oldid=4371358
sourceRevision=4371358
sourceRecordId=numbers:==Ordinal numbers==

Ordinal numerals in Russian are relatively easy to deal wit
originalSourceText===Ordinal numbers==

Ordinal numerals in Russian are relatively easy to deal with.  They all decline like adjectives.  For example: Только что фотографировала восемнадцатую девушку (She just photographed the eighteenth girl).

# п'''е'''рвый, п'''е'''рвая, п'''е'''рвое
# втор'''о'''й, втор'''а'''я, втор'''о'''е
# тр'''е'''тий, тр'''е'''тья, тр'''е'''тье
# четв'''ё'''ртый

recordType=instruction
sourceUrl=https://wisc.pb.unizin.org/diverserussian/chapter/russia-traditions-grammar/
sourceRevision=ab2170e37d529a318f395f6e657d8024d0eaed8d7c5c9b34f8831d348b8b76b3
sourceRecordId=pressbooks-traditions-grammar:Грамматика: At what time on the quarter hour</strong></p>
</header>
<div class="
originalSourceText=Грамматика: At what time on the quarter hour</strong></p>
</header>
<div class="textbox__content">
<table class="grid" style="border-collapse: collapse;width: 100%">
<thead>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>Time</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%"><strong>Explanation and examples</strong></td>
</tr>
</thead>
<tbody>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the hour (0.00)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>в</strong> + accusative, but note that the number then often requires genitive case after it. In informal speech, sometimes people leave out час / часа / часов. Remember: один час; два / три / четыре часа; пять часов.
<p>Концерт начинается <strong>в шесть часов</strong>. (18.00)<br>
Она была дома <strong>в час</strong>. (13.00)</p></td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the quarter hour (0.15)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>в</strong> + accusative with either <strong>четверть</strong> (quarter) or <strong>пятнадцать минут</strong>. Then you use the ordinal number of the next hour in the genitive case. In essence you are saying quarter of the next hour. Note that while you can say 6:15 as “шесть пятнадцать”, in the exercises on this page we would like to focus on this other way of expressing the time.
<p>Я приду <strong>в четверть восьмого</strong>. (7.15 – quarter of the eighth hour)<br>
Он нам позвонил <strong>в пятнадцать минут десятого</strong>. (9.15 – 15 minutes of the tenth hour)</p>
<p>If you need to review the ordinal numbers up to twelve, you can find them here:</p>
<div id="h5p-256">
<div class="h5p-iframe-wrapper"><iframe id="h5p-iframe-256" class="h5p-iframe" data-content-id="256" style="height:1px" src="about:blank" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="Ordinal numbers"></iframe></div>
</div>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the half hour (0.30)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>в</strong> + prepositional with <strong>половина</strong> and the genitive case of the ordinal number of the next hour, or colloquially, <strong>пол_____</strong> (genitive case of the ordinal number of the next hour). Note that the spelling of 10:30 adds a hyphen: пол-одиннадцатого.
<p>Наш рейс уезжает <strong>в половине пятого</strong>. (4.30 – half of the fifth hour)<br>
Мы будем свободны <strong>в полвторого</strong>. (1.30 – half of the second hour)</p>
<p>If you need to review the ordinal numbers up to twelve, you can find them here:</p>
<div id="h5p-256">
<div class="h5p-iframe-wrapper"><iframe id="h5p-iframe-256" class="h5p-iframe" data-content-id="256" style="height:1px" src="about:blank" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="Ordinal numbers"></iframe></div>
</div>
</td>
</tr>
<tr>
<td style="width: 33.3333%"><strong>At what time on the three quarters hour (0.45)</strong></td>
<td style="width: 66.6667%">Use <strong>без</strong> + genitive with <strong>четверть</strong> or <strong>пятнадцать минут</strong>. Then you use the cardinal number of the next hour in the nominative case. In essence you are saying X hours without X minutes.
<p>Передача начинается <strong>без четверти три</strong>. (2.45 – 3 without a quarter)<br>
Она обычно приходит на работу <strong>без пятнадцати девять</strong>. (8.45 – 9 without 15 minutes)</p>

sourceRecordId=interrogative-question-transfer:=== Который? ===
The primary meaning is simply 'which one?', though '''которы
originalSourceText==== Который? ===
The primary meaning is simply 'which one?', though '''который''' is also used to ask about one particular thing in a sequence of similar things.
:Which apple is mine? - '''Которое яблоко моё?'''
:What time is it? - '''Который час?'''
:Which book do you want? - '''Которую книгу вы хотите?'''

sourceRecordId=interrogative-question-transfer:=== Который? ===
The primary meaning is simply 'which one?', though '''которы
originalSourceText==== Который? ===
The primary meaning is simply 'which one?', though '''который''' is also used to ask about one particular thing in a sequence of similar things.
:Which apple is mine? - '''Которое яблоко моё?'''
:What time is it? - '''Который час?'''
:Which book do you want? - '''Которую книгу вы хотите?'''

recordType=instruction
sourceUrl=https://en.wikibooks.org/wiki/Russian/Vocabulary/Days_of_the_Week?oldid=3594124
sourceRevision=3594124
sourceRecordId=days:Russians don't capitalize days of the week.

{|
|-
| день || noun || day || dyeh
originalSourceText=Russians don't capitalize days of the week.

{|
|-
| день || noun || day || dyehn
|-
| colspan="4" | A cognate (same word in Russian and English).
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| сегодня || noun || today || sevódnya
|-
| colspan="4" | The г here is pronounced as a в. It sounds like "с его дня", which would mean "from his day", if день were an animate noun. But it's not.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| понедельник || noun || Monday || ponyedyél'nik
|-
| colspan="4" | On Mondays we ride our ''ponies'' to ''Nick's deli''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| вторник || noun || Tuesday || vtórnik
|-
| colspan="4" | On Tuesdays we go to the ''store'' with ''Nick''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| среда || noun || Wednesday || sryéda
|-
| colspan="4" | Wednesdays are a good day for ''shredding''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| четверг || noun || Thursday || chetvérg
|-
| colspan="4" | On Thursdays ''Chet'' goes to ''work''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| пятница || noun || Friday || pyátnitsa
|-
| colspan="4" | "On Fridays we eat ''pizza'' on a ''yacht'', ''neatly''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| суббота || noun || Saturday || soobbóta
|-
| colspan="4" | "On Saturdays ''Sue'' goes ''boating''. Also Saturday is the ''Sabbath''. Don't confuse суббота with собакa, that is a dog.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| воскресенье || noun || Sunday

originalSourceText=Russians don't capitalize days of the week.

{|
|-
| день || noun || day || dyehn
|-
| colspan="4" | A cognate (same word in Russian and English).
|-

|-
| сегодня || noun || today || sevódnya
|-
| colspan="4" | The г here is pronounced as a в. It sounds like "с его дня", which would mean "from his day", if день were an animate noun. But it's not.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| понедельник || noun || Monday || ponyedyél'nik
|-
| colspan="4" | On Mondays we ride our ''ponies'' to ''Nick's deli''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| вторник || noun || Tuesday || vtórnik
|-
| colspan="4" | On Tuesdays we go to the ''store'' with ''Nick''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| среда || noun || Wednesday || sryéda
|-
| colspan="4" | Wednesdays are a good day for ''shredding''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| четверг || noun || Thursday || chetvérg
|-
| colspan="4" | On Thursdays ''Chet'' goes to ''work''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| пятница || noun || Friday || pyátnitsa
|-
| colspan="4" | "On Fridays we eat ''pizza'' on a ''yacht'', ''neatly''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| суббота || noun || Saturday || soobbóta
|-
| colspan="4" | "On Saturdays ''Sue'' goes ''boating''. Also Saturday is the ''Sabbath''. Don't confuse суббота with собакa, that is a dog.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| воскресенье || noun || Sunday

|-

|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| среда || noun || Wednesday || sryéda
|-
| colspan="4" | Wednesdays are a good day for ''shredding''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| четверг || noun || Thursday || chetvérg
|-
| colspan="4" | On Thursdays ''Chet'' goes to ''work''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| пятница || noun || Friday || pyátnitsa
|-
| colspan="4" | "On Fridays we eat ''pizza'' on a ''yacht'', ''neatly''.
|-
| &nbsp;
|-
| суббота || noun || Saturday || soobbóta
|-
| colspan="4" | "On Saturdays ''Sue'' goes ''boating''. Also Saturday is the ''Sabbath''. Don't confuse суббота with собакa, that is a dog.
|-
| &nbsp;
